# The workshop: sampling by hand {.unnumbered} *This page is a record of what the first contact hour established, not a transcript of it. If you were there, read it to fix the conclusions. If you were not, work through @sec-catchup, which gets you the same object by a weaker route.* ## What we did Every bench had a tub holding several hundred dried beans of varying size. Before touching them, you each wrote down a single number: your best guess at the mean mass of every bean in the tub. One number, committed, with no data. You then drew five beans without looking, weighed them, and calculated the mean of your five. Those means went on the board, one per person. Then benches pooled their beans into samples of twenty and the exercise was repeated. Finally the true mean of the whole tub was revealed. ## What it established **Nobody's sample mean was the population mean.** Not one. This was not a failure of technique or a sign that anyone drew badly. Five beans cannot tell you the mean of eight hundred, and the arithmetic you performed on those five did not repair the fact. **The room produced a different answer to the same question every time.** Forty people, one identical procedure, forty different numbers. That is the point at which the sample mean stops being a fact about the tub and starts being a random variable, exactly as defined in the pre-class reading: a quantity settled by a random process, which comes out differently each time the process runs. **The cloud of means was narrower than the cloud of beans, and narrower again at n = 20.** The individual beans on the board spread across a wide range. The means of five occupied a much smaller stretch of the same axis, centred in the same place. The means of twenty were tighter still. Those three observations are the same three facts previewed in @sec-average, but you generated them rather than read them, which is the only reason the hour existed. ## The vocabulary, now fixed - **Population**: every bean in the tub. In real work, the thing you want to make a claim about and cannot measure. - **Sample**: the five you drew. - **Parameter**: a number describing the population, such as its true mean. Usually unknown. - **Statistic**: a number calculated from a sample, such as your sample mean. Known, and different every time. - **Data distribution**: the spread of the individual bean masses on the board. - **Sampling distribution**: the spread of the sample means on the board. A different object, on the same axis, and the one the rest of Block 1 is about. - **Sampling variability**: the fact that the statistic moves from sample to sample, which is what the width of the sampling distribution measures. ::: {.callout-warning} ## The mistake this hour exists to prevent It is easy to agree that samples differ and then, five minutes later, write your sample mean into a report as though it were the population value. Agreeing with the first sentence does not stop you doing the second. That is why the exercise was physical and why you committed to a number first. ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## What Session 2 adds We deliberately stopped short of a number. You saw that the sampling distribution is narrower than the data distribution, and narrower still with larger samples, but not by *how much*. The quantity that answers this is the **standard error**, and it is the first thing we do next session. Keep the distinction between it and the standard deviation of the beans clearly in view, because those two are the most commonly confused pair of numbers in applied biology. ::: ## Catch-up: if you missed the workshop {#sec-catchup} ::: {.callout-warning} ## This is a substitute, and a poor one The hour was physical and social. People visibly disagreeing about one number is not something a console reproduces, and the object you build below will be correct without being surprising. The tub simulated here is also not the tub that was in the room, so your numbers will resemble the board's without matching them. If you can, borrow a bench-mate's five bean masses and their committed guess before you start, and work through this with those. ::: Commit first, or the rest of this is pointless. The simulated tub below holds 800 beans with masses in grams. Beans of this kind mostly fall somewhere between 0.2 g and 1.2 g. ::: {.webex-check .webex-box} Before running anything: what do you think the mean mass of all 800 beans is, in grams to two decimal places?
Do not. The number is worth nothing to you; the gap between it and your guess is the entire content of the exercise.
::: Now build the tub and take one sample of five, which is what your hand did in the room. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} beans <- bean_population() my_sample <- beans |> slice_sample(n = 5) my_sample ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| bean_id| mass_g| |-------:|------:| | 191| 0.60| | 442| 0.59| | 237| 0.45| | 254| 0.24| | 18| 0.86|
::: ```{.r .cell-code} mean(my_sample$mass_g) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.548 ``` ::: ::: Run that block again. You will get a different five beans and a different mean. Run it a third time. That is the whole phenomenon. Now do what the room did collectively, forty times over. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} room <- withr::with_seed(demo_seed, { tibble( student = 1:40, sample_mean = map_dbl(1:40, \(i) mean(slice_sample(beans, n = 5)$mass_g)) ) }) ggplot(mapping = aes(x = mass_g)) + geom_histogram(data = beans, bins = 40, fill = house_col, alpha = 0.35) + geom_histogram( data = room |> rename(mass_g = sample_mean), bins = 40, fill = house_col ) + geom_vline(xintercept = mean(beans$mass_g), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) + labs(x = "Mass (g)", y = "Count") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The simulated room. Pale bars are 800 individual bean masses; dark bars are 40 sample means, each from a sample of five. The dashed line is the true population mean. The means are centred in the same place and occupy a far narrower stretch of the same axis.](01-workshop_files/figure-html/fig-catchup-means-1.png){#fig-catchup-means width=672} ::: ::: Two questions to answer for yourself in writing before you move on.
